newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Boeing move may aid Russia plane integration.
newsitem.headline: Boeing move may aid Russia plane integration.

text.p: Leading Russian plane manufacturers said on Monday that a merger between U.S. competitors Boeing Co and McDonnel Douglas Corp could also help boost integration within Russia.
Boeing, the world leader in commercial aviation, announced on Sunday its planned acquisition of McDonnell Douglas for 13 billion dollars.
Alexander Dondukov, Yakovlev corporation's chief designer, told Reuters that the world aviation industry was dividing into two strong regional groups based in the United States and in Europe.
"Sunday's news showed that the time for integration of Russian plane makers is approaching," he said.
"I see only one way to survive and that is integration. The merger of Boeing and McDonnel Douglas confirmed this."
Lev Lanovsky, chief designer at the Tupolev company, said that the U.S. companies' merger would not have an impact on Russia's aviation industry.
"It is a signal for Airbus Industrie which may meet some troubles soon," he said.
But he added that Russian airlines which planned to lease or buy Airbus-made planes would press ahead. "They will not change their position after the merger is fixed," he said.
"Of course, Boeing 777 jet is very promising plane, but A-330 and 340s are also competitive aircraft," Lanovsky added.
He also said that in 2-3 years a few models of Russian-made planes may also be competitve on the world market. He did not name the models.
Aeroflot and Transaero airlines senior officials were not available for immediate comment. A Transaero spokesman said the company president and his deputies were in the United States.
"They were invited by Boeing and McDonnell Douglas," he said. He gave no more details.
Currently Aeroflot-Russian International Airlines operates two Boeing 767s, one DC-10 cagro freighter and 10 A-310 passenger jets.
Earlier this year Aeroflot said it planned to buy 10 Boeing-737-400 jets at a total cost of $25-30 million.
Transaero has no Airbus-made planes and operates five Boeing 757s, five 737s and three wide-body DC-10-30 jets.
Alexander Smolko, Aeroflot-Leasing president, said that the U.S. merger set a good example for Russian aviation manufacturers, whose market he said remained on the "road to disintegration".
"This merger will make world competition much sharper and it is not good for Russia if our plane-makers do not unite," Smolko said.
